title: Editorial: Soundscape, well-being and mental health during/after the COVID-19 pandemic
central_proposition: This editorial introduces a research topic exploring how the COVID-19 pandemic and associated lockdowns altered acoustic environments and urban soundscapes, consequently impacting human perception, well-being, and mental health, and highlights the need for targeted interventions.

concept_definitions.name: Soundscape
concept_definitions.definition: The acoustic environment as perceived or experienced and/or understood by a person or people, in context. Used as an established concept in this paper.

concept_definitions.name: Well-being
concept_definitions.definition: A state of being comfortable, healthy, or happy. Used as an established concept in this paper, particularly in relation to environmental influences.

concept_definitions.name: Mental health
concept_definitions.definition: A person’s condition with regard to their psychological and emotional well-being. Used as an established concept in this paper, particularly in relation to environmental influences and psychological distress.

argument_structure: The editorial first establishes the COVID-19 pandemic as a major global health catastrophe and notes the end of its emergency phase. It then describes how strict lockdown measures, adopted to combat the pandemic, profoundly altered acoustic environments and urban soundscapes, subsequently impacting residents' sound perception, psychological distress, and overall physical and mental health. The paper then introduces the Research Topic's aim to explore these changes and potential interventions, summarizing seven published articles that contribute to this understanding, categorized by their focus on acoustic environment changes, human perception relationships, and subjective evaluations.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism involves the disruption of typical environmental statistics due to pandemic-induced lockdowns, leading to altered acoustic environments and urban soundscapes. These changes, in turn, influence residents' sound perception and, when combined with the psychological distress caused by regulations, negatively impact physical and mental health. Conversely, restorative soundscapes are proposed to mitigate these negative effects by providing positive sensory input and facilitating psychological states like privacy and intimacy.

findings.consequent: A-weighted sound pressure level (LAeq) in urban apartment buildings
findings.mechanism: Implied change in human activity patterns due to lockdown easing, leading to altered noise levels.
findings.source: section: Editorial on the Research Topic
findings.quote: the A-weighted sound pressure level (LAeq) of all 14 floors after the lockdown was higher than that during the lockdown.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Summarized from Yang and Kang (special issue paper).

findings.antecedent: satisfaction with indoor acoustic environment and odor in hospitals
findings.consequent: patients' perception of indoor environment as helpful in recovery from COVID-19
findings.mechanism: Sensory comfort (acoustic and olfactory) contributes to perceived restorativeness and healing processes in vulnerable populations.
findings.source: section: Editorial on the Research Topic
findings.quote: Satisfaction with the indoor acoustic environment and odor were significant predictors how patients perceived the indoor environment to be helpful in their recovery from COVID-19.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Summarized from Park et al. (special issue paper).

findings.antecedent: ideal indoor soundscape (quiet, well-sound insulated, access to positive sounds like natural sounds, music, urban background)
findings.consequent: privacy, intimacy, and freedom from noise-related constraints for self-expression
findings.mechanism: Reduced noise intrusion and the presence of desired sounds facilitate psychological states of privacy and intimacy, enabling unconstrained self-expression.
findings.source: section: Editorial on the Research Topic
findings.quote: The ideal soundscape was described as a quiet, well-sound insulated environment, which guarantees access to positive sounds (i.e., natural sounds, music, and urban background), thus resulting in privacy, intimacy, and a place to express themselves without noise-related constraints.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Summarized from Torresin et al. (special issue paper).

findings.consequent: environmental health indicators (willingness to walk, relaxation, safety, beauty, comprehensive comfort)
findings.mechanism: Traffic noise impacts multiple dimensions of perceived environmental quality and associated behaviors, influencing overall environmental health perception.
findings.source: section: Editorial on the Research Topic
findings.quote: The study by Ren et al. utilized five indicators (willingness to walk, relaxation, safety, beauty, and comprehensive comfort) to measure the environmental health of pedestrian streets with traffic noise.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Summarized from Ren et al. (special issue paper).

findings.consequent: individuals' perception of sound in urban residential environments at night
findings.mechanism: Multisensory integration, where visual cues from the environment can alter or influence auditory perception.
findings.source: section: Editorial on the Research Topic
findings.quote: visual elements can change individuals' perception of sound
findings.empirical_support_cited: Summarized from Yu et al. (special issue paper).

findings.antecedent: superposition of two intrusive variables (sound-light pollution)
findings.mechanism: Suggests that the combined effect of sound and light pollution might not linearly reduce tolerance, or other complex multisensory interactions are at play.
findings.source: section: Editorial on the Research Topic
findings.quote: but the tolerance limit of participants was not reduced due to the superposition of two intrusive variables.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Summarized from Yu et al. (special issue paper).

findings.antecedent: physical environment of elderly care facility dining rooms (including acoustic aspects) before and after COVID-19 pandemic
findings.mechanism: Environmental quality, including acoustic characteristics, influences the comfort and well-being of elderly residents during dining activities.
findings.source: section: Editorial on the Research Topic
findings.quote: The study by Mu and Kang is about the Dining comfort in elderly care facility dining rooms before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, by measuring the physical environment of the facilities, analyzing dining behavior, and surveying the elderly residents.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Summarized from Mu and Kang (special issue paper).

findings.antecedent: subjective factors and restorative effects of natural sounds
findings.mechanism: Subjective interpretation and exposure to restorative elements can buffer or moderate the negative impact of environmental stressors like aircraft noise.
findings.source: section: Editorial on the Research Topic
findings.quote: The findings implied the moderating effects of subjective factors and the restorative effects of natural sounds, which could inform aircraft noise control and community consultation strategies by protecting vulnerable populations and creating community soundscape facilities.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Summarized from Qu et al. (special issue paper).

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Targeted interventions and preventative measures designed to address the altered acoustic environment and soundscape during/after global health emergencies will positively impact residents' mental health and well-being.
The restorative effects of soundscapes can be leveraged to mitigate the psychological distress and negative health impacts experienced during and after periods of strict environmental regulations.
bridge_warrants: The editorial connects environmental psychology (soundscape perception, acoustic environment) with public health and urban planning by demonstrating how environmental changes impact psychological distress, physical health, and well-being.

It highlights the interplay between individual attributes and environmental factors in shaping human perception and health outcomes, bridging individual differences research with environmental design.
